n: David escapes to the cave of Adullam in the hills of Judah. His brothers and family join him, probably because Saul's anger now endangers them too.

f.g: Adullam was a town in the Judean lowlands; the area has many caves. The headings of Psalms 57 and 142 mention David “in the cave.”

n: About four hundred men gather to David: people in distress, in debt, or bitter about their lives. David turns these outcasts into a loyal band — a sign of his gift for leadership.
David takes his parents to Moab for safety. Since his great-grandmother Ruth was a Moabite, he may have had family ties there.

f.g: A place in Moab, not the Mizpeh in Benjamin.

n: David's parents stay with the king of Moab as long as David remains in his stronghold.

f.g: the stronghold, a fortified hiding place

n: The prophet Gad tells David not to stay in the stronghold but to return to Judah. David obeys and goes to the forest of Hareth. Even as a fugitive, David follows prophetic counsel.
Saul hears where David is. The scene shows Saul sitting under a tree at Gibeah, spear in hand, surrounded by his officials — a picture of a suspicious, insecure king.

f.g: Better “on the height” — a hill at Gibeah.

n: Saul appeals to tribal loyalty: will David, from Judah, give you Benjaminites fields and promotions like I have? He is buying loyalty through favoritism.
Saul accuses them of conspiracy and self-pityingly complains that no one told him about Jonathan's covenant with David. His paranoia twists friendship into treason.

f.w: none of you that is sorry for me
f.g: no one feels concern for me

n: Doeg the Edomite speaks up, reporting that he saw David at Nob with Ahimelech.
Doeg reports that Ahimelech consulted the Lord for David and gave him food and Goliath's sword. His half-truth makes the priest sound like a conspirator.
Saul summons Ahimelech and all his family of priests at Nob, and they come.
Saul addresses Ahimelech coldly as “son of Ahitub,” and the priest answers respectfully.
Saul accuses Ahimelech of conspiring with David by giving him supplies and seeking God's guidance for him.
Ahimelech answers honestly: who among your servants is more faithful than David, your son-in-law, captain of your guard, and honored in your house?
He explains that inquiring of God for David was nothing new, and he knew nothing of any conflict. He asks the king not to blame him or his family.
Saul ignores the defense and sentences Ahimelech and his entire family to death.
Saul orders his guards to kill the Lord's priests, but they refuse to raise a hand against them. Their quiet courage contrasts with the king's madness.

f.w: would not put forth their hand

n: Saul turns to Doeg, the foreigner, who kills eighty-five priests. The massacre fulfills, in part, the prophecy against Eli's house.
Doeg also destroys the whole town of Nob — men, women, children, and animals. Saul inflicts on his own priests the total destruction he refused to carry out on Amalek.

f.w: both men and women, children and sucklings

n: One son of Ahimelech, Abiathar, escapes and flees to David. He will serve as David's priest for many years.
Abiathar tells David that Saul has killed the Lord's priests.
David takes responsibility: he saw Doeg that day and knew he would report it. He admits his actions led to the deaths of Abiathar's family. Honest accountability is a mark of David's best character.

f.g: I am responsible for the death

n: David invites Abiathar to stay with him, promising protection. They share the same enemy, and David will keep him safe.
